## The big idea

If our submerged body has a hinge, we might need to think about moments instead of simple forces. No problem! The framework we have built up for creating integrals applies here as well, we just need to figure out the "lever arm" and then compute a cross product within the integrand.

## Think first

**Recall**

1. Moments are force times distance, but in vector calculus we use the cross product, $\mathbf{r}\wedge \mathbf{F}$ ... displacement crossed with force.

**Look ahead**

1. How do we modify our force integrals (the ones with the surface normal) to include another vector quantity: the lever arm?


## A force example

We covered this one in class, but let's do it again here.

A pool has depth $H$, and its bottom right corner is a quarter-cylinder with radius $R<H$ and length $L$. Determine the force, including direction, on the corner section.

We need to figure out all the terms in

$$
    \mathbf{F}=\int -p(\mathbf{x})\hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{x})dA
$$

at which point Wolfram Alpha or Desmos or whatever can handle the math. For our purposes, it will make sense to define a polar coordinate system around the curved section, with center located at a depth $H-R$.

**Determine the best way to write $dA$**. The quarter-cylinder is easily represented in terms of cylindrical coordinates, with the surface being located at a constant radius $R$. We'll use $dA = R \,d\theta \, dz$.

**Write pressure in these coordinates**. Pressure still depends only on depth. We have options for how to define $\theta$ (and I can't remember what we did in class!)... let's say $\theta =0$ at the deepest part of the pool and increases to $\theta=\pi/2$ at the end of the quarter-cylinder. Then:

$$
p(\theta) = \rho g \left(H-R + R\cos\theta\right).
$$

Some sanity checks:

- When $\theta=0$, we should have that the depth is $H$. Indeed: $\cos(0)=1$, and our depth is $H-R+R=H$.
- When $\theta = \pi/2$, we should have that the depth is $H-R$. Indeed: $\cos(\pi/2)=0$, and our depth is $H-R+0= H-R$.

I'm satisfied.

**Determine the surface normal**. We'll use the normal that points *into* the fluid (hence the negative sign out-front of the integral — the force pushes against that normal). We should have been more precise in the original problem statement: we are looking for the $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$- and $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$-components of force, defining $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ as to the right and $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ as upwards. We suspect the unit circle will be relevant, so let's guess (incorrectly, we will see) the standard definition:

$$
\hat{\mathbf{n}} = \left\langle \cos\theta, \sin\theta \right\rangle.
$$

Some sanity checks:

- When $\theta=0$, we should have $\hat{\mathbf{n}}=\hat{\mathbf{y}}$. Actually, we get $\left\langle 1,0 \right\rangle$, so it seems we have our sine and cosine flipped. Guess better:

$$
\hat{\mathbf{n}} = \left\langle \sin\theta, \cos\theta \right\rangle.
$$

Some sanity checks:

- When $\theta=0$, we should have $\hat{\mathbf{n}}=\hat{\mathbf{y}}$. We get $\left\langle 0,1 \right\rangle$, great.
- When $\theta=\pi/2$, we should have $\hat{\mathbf{n}}=-\hat{\mathbf{x}}$. We get $\left\langle 1,0 \right\rangle$, which has the wrong sign. Flipping the $x$-component (and only that one) fixes it.

So I think this is going to be our **actual** normal vector:

$$
\hat{\mathbf{n}} = \left\langle -\sin\theta, \cos\theta \right\rangle.
$$

**Build the integral, including the bounds**. We've got

$$
\begin{align*}
\mathbf{F}&=\int -p(\mathbf{x})\hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{x})dA\\
&= - \int\limits_0^L \int\limits_0^{\pi/2} \rho g \left(H-R + R\cos\theta\right) \left\langle -\sin\theta, \cos\theta \right\rangle R \,d\theta \,dz.
\end{align*}
$$

which is something we can indeed calculate: it's technically two integrals, one for each component, but Wolfram Alpha has no trouble with it.


::: {.callout-important}
I'm trying to instill this perspective: comprehending and setting-up a problem is far more valuable than completing the calculation. Too often I have heard students say "I just used Chegg/ChatGPT to get started, I did the math myself"... honestly, once the integral is set up, I don't care if you use a computer to do the calculus. The wisdom that goes into understanding the problem and getting into a calculable form is *vastly* more important than your ability to remember the integrals of trigonometric functions.
:::



## Moments

We calculated (vector) forces using

$$
\mathbf{F}=\int -p(\mathbf{x})\hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{x})dA.
$$

To get (vector) moments, we need to fit the "force $\times$ distance" into the integrand. We'll have an infinitesimal force, $-p(\mathbf{x})\hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{x})dA$, and we'll use $\mathbf{r}$ as our displacement vector. Remember that when dealing with vectors, moments are actually "distance $\times$ force", and so our integral is

$$
\mathbf{M}=\int -\mathbf{r}\wedge p(\mathbf{x})\hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{x})dA
$$

where I used $\wedge$ for the cross product symbol, to make it distinct from $\mathbf{x}$ (which looks too much like $\times$).

### Moment example 1

Let's do a basic one but with our vector calculus notation: remember the problem with a gate on an angled wall? We computed the torque needed to keep it closed in [Torques from pressure distributions](../unit-3/p-int.qmd#torques-from-pressure-distributions), using a scalar lever arm. Here was the figure:


A scalar perspective was fine because the force and displacement were perpendicular, and so the moment was simply the product of those two quantities. Let's redo it with the vector formula:

$$
\mathbf{M}=\int -\mathbf{r}\wedge p(\mathbf{x})\hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{x})dA.
$$

**The unit normal**. Even though we integrated $dy'\,dz$, we can still write this in terms of the $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$- and $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$-components:

$$
\hat{\mathbf{n}}=\left\langle -\cos\beta, \sin\beta \right\rangle
$$

is going to be the vector pointing into the fluid, assuming we are thinking about the horizontal and vertical components. Some sanity checks:

- When $\beta=0$, the wall is vertical with the fluid on its left, so we should have $\hat{\mathbf{n}}=-\hat{\mathbf{x}}$. We get $\left\langle -1, 0\right\rangle$, great.
- When $\beta=\pi/4$, the wall leans away from the fluid, so the normal into the fluid should point left and up. We get $\left\langle -\sqrt{2}/2, \sqrt{2}/2\right\rangle$. Great.

::: {.column-margin}
Be careful here: we measured *depth* $y$ as being downwards (so that $p=\rho g y$), but this normal vector is still thinking about the rightward component and the upward component. There is not necessarily a contradiction, just be clear about what you are reporting (e.g., with a note like this one!).
:::

**The displacement vector.** If we are going to stick with "the rightward component" and "the upward component", then the displacement from the hinge needs a length and a direction. The hinge is at $y'=H_\text{hinge}/\cos\beta$, so a point on the gate at $y'$ is a distance $H_\text{hinge}/\cos\beta-y'$ from it, and the direction from the hinge up the wall is $\left\langle \sin\beta,\ \cos\beta\right\rangle$ (the wall leans to the right by $\beta$ as it goes up). Thus

$$
\mathbf{r}=\left(\frac{H_\text{hinge}}{\cos\beta}-y'\right)
\left\langle \sin\beta,\ \cos\beta\right\rangle.
$$

Check: when $\beta=0$, this is a vector pointing straight up from the hinge, which makes sense because the gate is above the hinge.

**The cross product.** In two dimensions, the cross product of $\left\langle a,b\right\rangle$ and $\left\langle c,d\right\rangle$ has only a $z$-component (out of the page): $ad-bc$. So

$$
\mathbf{r}\wedge\hat{\mathbf{n}} = \left(\frac{H_\text{hinge}}{\cos\beta}-y'\right)\left[\sin\beta\cdot\sin\beta - \cos\beta\cdot(-\cos\beta)\right]
= \left(\frac{H_\text{hinge}}{\cos\beta}-y'\right).
$$

(The bracket is $\sin^2\beta+\cos^2\beta=1$.) Now we plug into the moment integral, with $p=\rho g\cos\beta\,y'$, $dA=dy'\,dz$, and the gate (recall that it has length $\ell$ along the wall and width $W$ into the page) spanning $y'$ from $H_\text{hinge}/\cos\beta-\ell$ to $H_\text{hinge}/\cos\beta$ and $z$ from $0$ to $W$:

$$
M_z = -\int\limits_0^W\int\limits_{H_\text{hinge}/\cos\beta-\ell}^{H_\text{hinge}/\cos\beta} \left(\frac{H_\text{hinge}}{\cos\beta}-y'\right)\left(\rho g \cos\beta\, y'\right) dy'\,dz.
$$

This is exactly the scalar integral from before, with a minus sign in front: same magnitude, and now the sign tells us the direction. With $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ to the right, $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ up, and $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ out of the page, a negative $M_z$ is *clockwise*. That makes sense: the water pushes the gate to the right and down, into the wall, and the gate is above and to the right of the hinge, so it wants to rotate clockwise.

::: {.callout-note}
We could have also written these in terms of our new coordinate $y'$, though we'd need to use a perpendicular coordinate $x'$ to make the description legal. That is: we could write
 
$$
\hat{\mathbf{n}} = \left\langle n_{x'}, n_{y'} \right\rangle.
$$

Since $\hat{\mathbf{y}}'$ goes down the surface, and if we define $\hat{\mathbf{x}}'$ as being perpendicular to that going into the fluid:

$$
\hat{\mathbf{n}} = \left\langle 1, 0 \right\rangle
$$

and, since the gate is *above* the hinge (at a smaller $y'$),

$$
\mathbf{r}= \left\langle 0,\ y'-\frac{H_\text{hinge}}{\cos\beta} \right\rangle.
$$

Then $\mathbf{r}\wedge\hat{\mathbf{n}} = 0\cdot 0 - \left(y'-H_\text{hinge}/\cos\beta\right)(1) = H_\text{hinge}/\cos\beta-y'$, the same as before, as it has to be: it doesn't matter which (right-handed) coordinate system we use to compute the cross product.
:::


### Moment example 2

I don't want to give away too much — the homework problem will be similar! But let's look at [the force example from above](#a-force-example) and think about what would happen if there was a hinge located on the bottom, at $\theta=0$.

Differential area, pressure distribution, normal vector, bounds of integration — all the same. The only thing we need to figure out is how to write the moment arm $\mathbf{r}$ from hinge to an arbitrary point on the surface.

An intuitive way to think about it: trace to the origin on our coordinate system, then out to the arbitrary point. To go from the hinge back to the origin, we take vector displacement $\left\langle 0, R\right\rangle$. Then to go out to an arbitrary point on the surface, we do a little trig to find

$$
\mathbf{r} = \left\langle 0, R\right\rangle + 
\left\langle R\sin\theta, -R\cos\theta\right\rangle.
$$


::: {.callout-note}
The definition of $\theta=0$ pointing downwards creates confusion here, too — again we have sine, -cosine instead of cosine, sine. Don't trust trigonometry! The most deceitful field of mathematics! Make little sketches/check values... it won't take long.
:::

With this, we will again arrive at a mathematical equation that is easily handled by Wolfram Alpha — just remember your cross product rules!
